content: The Japan Anti-Tuberculosis Association, represented by Alaine Umubyeyi Nyaruhirira from Management Sciences for Health in South Africa, Rohit Sarin from the LRS Institute of TB and Respiratory Diseases in India, and Alena Shrahina from the National TB Program in Belarus, contributed to the development of these guidelines. The systematic review team included Karen Steingart from the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, USA, and Grant Theron from Stellenbosch University, South Africa. Observers such as Sevim Ahmedov (USAID, USA), Emmanuelle Cambau (Groupe Hospitalier Lariboisière-Fernand Widal, France), Miranda Langendam (University of Amsterdam, Netherlands), Thomas Schön (Kalmar County Hospital and Linköping University, Sweden), and Belay Tessema (FIND, Switzerland) also participated. Funding for this work was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and USAID through the USAID–WHO consolidated grant (GHA-G-00-09-00003/US-2014-741). The development of the lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay section was overseen by Christopher Gilpin and Alexei Korobitsyn, with input from Annabel Baddeley, Licé González-Angulo, and Fuad Mirzayev from the WHO Global TB Programme, as well as Meg Doherty, Satvinder Singh, and Lara Vojnov from the WHO HIV Department. Coordination was led by Karin Weyer under the direction of Tereza Kasaeva, Director of the WHO Global TB Programme. The guidelines were drafted by Alexei Korobitsyn with contributions from Annabel Baddeley, Christopher Gilpin, and Lara Vojnov, based on consensus achieved during the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting held from May 14–16, 2019. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics represent the third edition of such guidelines. Compared to the second edition issued in 2022, this document introduces a new chapter on targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) tests for diagnosing drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) in individuals with TB, with or without rifampicin resistance (RR-TB). The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for novel diagnostic tools to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and mutations associated with anti-TB drug resistance. The target audience for these guidelines includes laboratory managers, clinicians, healthcare staff, HIV and TB program managers, policymakers, technical agencies, donors, and implementing partners working in resource-limited settings. The document is also relevant for individuals involved in program planning, budgeting, resource mobilization, and training activities for managing DR-TB. The WHO’s End TB Strategy emphasizes early diagnosis of TB and universal drug susceptibility testing (DST), highlighting the critical role of laboratories in rapidly and accurately detecting TB and drug resistance. The guidelines include recommendations for various diagnostic technologies, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), line probe assays (LPAs), and targeted NGS. These technologies are evaluated based on their ability to detect TB and drug resistance efficiently and accurately. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay, developed by Cepheid, marked a significant advancement in TB diagnosis and rifampicin resistance detection. However, its sensitivity is suboptimal, particularly in smear-negative and HIV-associated TB cases. To address these limitations, Cepheid developed the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay, which uses the same GeneXpert platform but offers improved sensitivity. The guidelines also discuss the use of moderate-complexity automated NAATs, which are faster and less complex than phenotypic culture-based DST and LPAs. These tests can serve as initial diagnostic tools for detecting TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid. Additionally, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) is highlighted as a low-complexity technology suitable for implementation at the lowest levels of laboratory networks, although it does not detect resistance-associated mutations. Urinary LF-LAM assays, while not suitable as standalone diagnostic tests for TB in all populations due to suboptimal sensitivity and specificity, show improved sensitivity for diagnosing TB in individuals co-infected with HIV. A new class of low-complexity automated NAATs is also introduced for rapid DST in intermediate and peripheral laboratories, offering results in under 90 minutes. Targeted NGS tests represent a new class of diagnostics capable of detecting resistance to a broader range of drugs, including new and repurposed drugs not covered by other molecular assays. These tests offer comprehensive resistance detection aligned with modern treatment regimens and may provide better accuracy than existing WHO-recommended diagnostic tests. Regulatory approval is required before implementing these new diagnostic tools. The guidelines provide detailed recommendations for initial and repeat diagnostic testing for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, tailored to specific testing technologies and patient populations.
